other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2023-05-28", "text": "As I noted a year ago, my new strategy for keeping animal pests away from my melons is to put a plastic bucket over each one, with a brick on top. A 1-2 gallon bucket is about right. Time to get out the buckets. I used to battle raccoons and possums regularly for these melons. I often knew when a melon was ripe, because I'd come out and there was a big bite taken out of it. Canteloupes are especially risky in this regard because they SMELL ripe. They self-invite pilfering. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-03-01", "text": "The species that is considered invasive here is Clematis orientalis. C. tangutica does look similar to orientalis but has bell shaped, nodding flowers of a brighter yellow and slightly toothed leaves. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-94497977", "author_name": "Marie K", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-94497977", "date": "2025-05-04", "text": "I will answer some of these questions as an Invisacook owner of over a year. Cookware: The pot and pan set MUST MUST MUST BE 5-PLY or 7-ply (or test a really realy good 3-ply maybe with copper core?) stainless for optimum performance. 3-ply mid-class brands definitely do not perform as fast or as good, and depending on the brand, as evenly dispersed in heating.  At first I had a \"middle-cheap\" highly reviewed induction cookware set, terrible.  I ditched that stepping up to Caraway, and that performs well enough, but still not a top performer.  So plan on an extra 500-1000 for a really good cookware set, in addition to your cooktop cost. Cast iron does work but the 5-ply stainless seems to distribute heat around the pan better than cast iron (which seams counterintuitive to me).  I do have a knock-off enameled cast iron set I love, but I mostly reserve it for baking.  For the cooktop I do use it for things like chili and a huge pot of pasta sauce for example.  The cast iron throws off more heat, and I believe more heat is wasted into the room, is part of the issue.  Invisacook says something about that too. Tests mentioned above by others, I believe, do not mention exactly which type  and make and brand of pot used.  Temperature of ingoing water, ambient temperature, type of pot, if lid is used, type of porcelain and thickness and quality of porcelain, if the appliance is already warmed up, if power boost is used, if it is wired to 240v, all and more will all affect results in tests.  More on test below, but first here is a bit of results using less than ideal pans: TEST results of pans NOT recommended for illustration and learning, different mid-quality brands: ALL TESTS ARE AT AMBIENT TEMPERATURE OF 68F / 20C ALL TESTS ARE WITH WATER TEMPERATURE OF ABOUT 50F / 10C All but one test is with no lid, as lid will speed up performance markedly First enameled cast iron: Taking my 8 inch wide \"knock-off (copy) Le Crueset\" enameled cast iron frying pan cold, NO lid, using one cup by volume  (quarter liter) , time to simmer was a minute -- yes a single minute -- and boiling in a minute and about 15 seconds. Taking my 10 inch wide \"Le Crueset copy\" enameled cast iron sauce pan, cold, NO lid, using 4 cups by volume water (just shy of one liter), water reached simmer in about 5 minutes and boiling in about 7 minutes. This time is vastly reduced with a lid. Caraway (expensive) and inexpensive cookware (Carote): Trying a CARAWAY saucepan, 3 quarts (under 3 liters), cold, WITH LID because no lid is painfully slow!!! 4 cups by volume water (just shy of one liter), time to reach simmer was over 15 minutes (!!!) and boiling about 17.5 minutes.=( Note that this single pan costs well over $100 !!!  This is NOT a cheap pan! Yet it performs horribly. My lower-grade inexpensive induction cookware set I had at the start performed even worse. -- that was a Carote set, took over a half hour for the same amount of water and the same size pan as this Caraway test.   I got rid of those right away.  I did not realize then that the highest end cookware really does make a huge difference. I have a 3-ply stainless 12 inch frying pan that performs fast like the enameled cast iron, but again has the center hot spot and outer cold spots, rendering it fairly useless at that size. I NOTE THAT IN MY BOILING TEST in my \"not recommended\" enameled cast iron that I can see the ring on the bottom of the pan of bubbles hugging the pan surface, the subsurface bubbles, that is LESS than the diameter of the pan. In other words, I can view the BURNER RING working through the pan, evidence that the heat is NOT distributing around the pan's bottom surface but is instead distributing through the WATER itself.  THAT IS WHY THE CAST IRON IS NOT RECOMMENDED AND 5-PLY or better IS RECOMMENDED.  So with pots of soup or pasta water and so on, these pans are fine.  But if you want to fry an egg or a steak or a veggie patty, you will have cold spots in the pan. THIS IS WHY I SAY 5-PLY or better stainless IS A MUST, at least with pan simmer or frying where even heat by the pan itself is crucial.  It will distribute the heat across the pan cooking surface and allow pan searing and frying or even simmering. I though about ordering the 5-ply copper core Invisacook set itself, because there are risers attached to the bottom that do 2 things:  they are the points of heat distribution, ensuring that the heat is distributed FULLY AROUND the pan's cooking surface, and also the built in risers keep the counter cool thus nothing dripping over will slighly cook onto the surface requiring scrubbing, and thus no mats needed.  But this set ONLY comes in nonstick, and I am trying to stay away from nonstick.  Even if it does not leach into my food, it leaches into our water supply at both manufacturing and disposal, and nonstick does not last a lifetime. Ultimately I have decided on mostly Demeyer brand 5 and 7-ply, with a couple of other makes for various needs. Use of pads: You can cook on your counter without the pads and the counter does not get so hot in those spots that it would burn you.  It gets very warm, or decently hot like a sidewalk, but if a child touched it after moving the hot pan it will not burn.   It gets as hot as heat \"bleeding\" from the pot lets it get, so it also depends on the type of pan/pot. I have tried other silicone protective mats and they do work for counter protection.  But the Invisacook mats are designed to keep heat from \"throwing itself downward\" into your counter surface, further protecting your counter from long term heat exposure.  Of course porcelain can in fact take heat, it is a very high fired heat making process, and is much more vitrified than other ceramics from the super high kiln temperatures. I do in fact use their mats mainly because the hot pot bottom would itself slightly cook spillover into the surface requiring scrubbing.  I find my biggest incentive to use the mats is that I don't have to scrub the counter afterwards.  I am not sure it adds to heat conservation INSIDE the pot / pan or not, I cannot tell the difference regarding that.  I intend to run a test soon though. Burner Size and Power Boost: I have the 4-burner square.  Note that the 4-burner square has 2 larger burners and 2 smaller burners.  Note what type of unit you are considering to consider the amount of power reaching each burner.  There is also the power boost function, for liquid in the pan, not for heating for an oil fry.  So it says to only use it for water, but I find it helps also for starting big pots of broth for soup and so on.  I think it is meant to warn against too much food particulate matter in the pot when on power boost so that it does not burn on the bottom. Replacement: You absolutely can replace the unit without damaging your countertop.  And you absolutely can later cut out the counter in place to place inside a conventional cooktop, but you would need an expert counter/ porcelain tile person to do that, using specific blades and saws since they would not be using their wet saw for that.  It would take a bit to do it but could absolutely be done. Granite as a countertop option Yes indeed you can use granite WITH CAVEATS (keep reading).  I had in fact chosen a very specific slab of granite to install.  I chose it to blend with my soapstone counters that surround my cooking island, and it was understated and beautifully charcoal without much patter, just beautiful.  The counter stone place said that we should test it because if it has high iron, the heat will instead veer off into the counter surrounding the burners more than the pot, that it would not provide enough conductivity into the pot.  SOME GRANITE HAS TOO MUCH IRON CONTENT to be effective.  So we planned a test. They cut a small square of the slab, and milled it to the correct thickness (thinness).  I brought down a pot (a cheap one, my first terrible set).  They set the slab on top of the unit.  We poured in the water.  And just a few minutes later, it was a rolling boil, so fast!!  I was so happy, it worked fantastically well, almost indiscernible from a regular cooktop!! I walked away to the office to complete the purchase of the slab and waited for the staff.  About 15 minutes later, one of the crew came running in saying to come look at the slab, hurry!  So I did, as did the owner guy who had set up the test.  The slab piece had a fine crack developing.... from releasing water content! SOME GRANITE HAS REMAINING \"INVISIBLE\" WATER CONTENT THAT NEEDS EXPRESSING OUTWARD, OR TIME WITH LOW HEAT TO DRY IT OUT, or the slab will crack. So the summary on granite is:  It could possibly perform better than porcelain, but the slab must be cut for a test-piece, milled, hooked up to 240V and tested, to see if there is high iron content (or figure another way to test for iron?).  And then one must wait perhaps 30 minutes to see if the slab-piece cracks.  Or find granite slabs stored in a hot dry zone. Power Must be 240v, you must upgrade if necessary.  Must be on its own breaker, so make sure you have breaker space, or you have to upgrade that as well.    I would NOT choose the 110v version unless you were outfitting a small au pair suite or something and really did not want the added power there and do not mind the added time for cooking (versus not having cooking as an option for the space).  In other words I would only choose 110v if it was a choice of no cooking at all versus that, but then i would probably just choose a portable induction unit unless you were outfitting for more luxury. Power control I cut out a decent amount of the backside of a shallow top drawer about 30 inches wide, that is directly under the unit.  I mounted the control panel in that drawer, centered in the front of the drawer with a wood frame built around it to secure it into place and keep it from traveling around the drawer.    The edges of that frame happen to fall in line with the center line of the burners, and so it is super easy for me to find the burner location by glancing at the corner of that frame and running a mental line straight up onto the counter, and centering my pot on that line, either about 4 inches inward (wherever you mount it, you will adjust), or another pot width beyond that for the rear burners. The drawer gets warm so I do not keep anything else in that drawer but you could keep hot pads in there. Then I have large drawers under the control panel drawer, for pots and pans. Exhaust Fan I recommend a ceiling flush mount fan.  I have the Victory Sunset and absolutely love it.  We have enough windows that I don't have to use it often, but in the winter it is heaven to have such a great fan.  It works really fast, and is mounted at over 9 feet high, or about 6 feet above the surface of the counter. Ease of counter switch to serving and other uses I LOVE this aspect of the Invisacook.  I have a smallish to middle size house (for America, probably average for much of country-not-city-Europe) and need every surface.  My remodel made things work much much better, but when 10-20 people visit for a large meal, I absolutely need my island to convert to buffet serve.  And it is so easy to do that!  As things are plated, the counter is quickly wiped without waiting, the silicone pad is dropped in the drawer below, and the conversion to service area is in .motion.  Once the service line begins no one can tell it was just a cooktop.  It is fully a serving island, pots and pans in the sink out of the way. Also grocery loads can just pile all over the island, no wobbly parts from sitting on burners where they should not be anyway.  And occasionally other projects can take place easily on the counter surface. Porcelain choice I would probably go with whom they suggest, or run a test of different porcelain possibilites (as I suggest you do with the granite) so see if there is a difference in performance.  I don't know enough about porcelain qualities to advise on that but suspect there could be minor differences from cheap to quality porcelains. ___ Ok, I hope this helps someone.  This is all I wish I knew ahead of time.  Good luck to all searching.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "seniorballoon", "author_name": "SeniorBalloon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seniorballoon", "date": "2023-03-03", "text": "I have Michael Dirr's \"Manual of Woody Landscape Plants\". What other books would you recommend? In Dirr's book I went looking for clematis, and he has very little on propagation of clematis. I know there is lots of information on the net, but it's not always as detailed or informative as I'm looking for. What do professionals have on their bookshelf? Thanks.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "erasmus-gw", "author_name": "erasmus_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/erasmus-gw", "date": "2023-03-08", "text": "I have a number of books about Clematis and almost all of them have a section devoted to propagation techniques.   So you might  get yourself a few clematis books...they are wonderful to  look through.   I have some in my car where I can read if I'm waiting on someone,  or  take to a dr. appointment.    Some beautiful books can be had on ebay at great prices...usually under five dollars including shipping. Most of these books  say to take semi-ripe cuttings.   I have taken many cuttings myself and  currently have about   20+  tiny clematis plants coming along which were rooted last summer and fall.   I  agree with most books on the semi-ripe part.   You know how clematis stems become brown as they age?   Well,   I take cuttings when they're  not quite brown.   You don't want them too soft either.   The cuttings I take are pretty small...I cut just below a node and then  above the node and  trim any leaves to about two leaves.   I scrape  lightly  through the  outer \" bark\"  for about 1/2\",  put  rooting hormone powder on them and bury the node in pure sand with  the leaves sticking out above the sand.   Keep moist ,  put in  dappled light or am sun and leave them alone  for a couple of months.  In hot weather I use a misting system. If you root some and  leave them outside in winter,   know that in spring  it can take some time for some varieties to show new growth.   So don't assume they're dead .   Just wait awhile  to see if new growth pokes out.   I  really like  being able to root them because it takes some of the anxiety out of  planting .   If a plant doesn't make it in one spot a backup plant might make it in another.  It seems the most vigorous clems are the easiest to root...Polish Spirit and Triternata rubromarginata root  readily for example.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "john-magon", "author_name": "John Magon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/john-magon", "date": "2023-03-03", "text": "I am currently replacing my roof,I have a 70s ultra low pitch roof (2 degrees) the current minimum is 3 and many roofing manufacturers recommend nothing below 5 degrees. The existing roof is brown built long run roofing, a common standing seam roof used in the 70s.I have found in winter that there is condensation dripping off the roof underlay onto the insulation which is only a few centimetres below the roof. this massively reduces the R value of the insulation and causing mould to form on the ceiling. As it isn't drying out.As I will be replacing the roof, roof underlay and support mesh and insulation are there any ways to stop this?I am looking at thermocraft covertech 201And placing cavity batterns between the roof and underlay to help dry it out, could some insulation be placed directly under the roofing underlay to stop condensation forming, in a way moving the dew point closer to the outside. Is there a product suitable for this?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "agency-architecture-pfvwus-pf~1636377335", "author_name": "Agency Architecture", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/architectural-designer/agency-architecture-pfvwus-pf~1636377335", "date": "2023-05-01", "text": "Thank you for sharing your experience with condensation forming on your low-pitch roof, and for reaching out for advice on how to prevent this from happening during your roof replacement. One possible solution could be to add venting cavity battens on top of the purlins, which would allow for ventilation and help to reduce condensation. This would create a small air gap between the roof underlay and the insulation, which would allow for any moisture to escape. Additionally, using a suitable roof underlay, such as the Thermocraft Covertech 201 that you mentioned, could also help to prevent moisture from penetrating into the insulation. Overall, it's important to consult with a professional roofer or contractor who can recommend the best course of action based on your specific situation and the type of roofing materials being used. main_question: {"author_id": "taltalita", "author_name": "taltalita", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/taltalita", "date": "2023-03-03", "text": "Really hoping for clarity here... We have a 100 year old house with calcimine ceilings. Three large rooms in particular (dining room and two larger bedrooms) are in bad shape, with lots of cracking and some peeling. That said, some areas of the ceilings are fine (some rooms are worse / better than others). All the paint looked good when we moved in 10 years ago, thanks to touchups - we found the painter who did it... We had 4 companies come in, and ended up with three different proposals, varying in price of course. Each claiming theirs is the way to do it. We have no idea who's telling us the right approach. Help??? (1) Scrape only the peeling/cracked areas, then apply a bonding layer, then repaint over everything. Claim is that the areas that look fine now won't start peeling in a year because they're fine (we've been here 10 years), so only the areas that are cracking / peeling need scraping and a bonding layer. (2) Scrape everything (the whole ceiling), apply a bonding layer (or two, I forget), then apply the Benjamin Moore calcimine  paint as the last layer. Apparently has bad VOCs for a few hours, and also lots of dust from the scraping (the kids and one parent can be away that week, but there will still be cats and one person staying behind in the house). (3) Most expensive: new sheetrock for all the ceilings. We have some crown molding, so it's quite an expensive solution. If the cheap option (1) with the least dust and scraping is good enough, obviously that's what we'd want. But not sure I trust it to last?For option (2), how bad is the dust / VOCs? Does it work long term? We'd like it to look good for at least 12 years...Would really love some insight. Wind gusts over 70mph were recorded and that is pretty impressive when it includes heavy rain and lightning. We planted a lovely lacebark elm about fifteen years ago, an Ulmus parvifolia \u201dAllee\u201d, for those in the know.  These trees are very muscular, wide spreading and enormously beautuful.  They are also small in stature, making them a perfect candidate for a smallish front yard.   We planted it to get some relief from the Alabama western sun that baked our from door so extremely that we couldn\u2019t touch the door handles with bare fingers.    The sun made afternoons in the living room almost unlivable. Until the we planted that tree.  It grew about three feet per year in our Alabama red clay soil, without much from us other than plenty of water and lots of sweet talk and compliments. After it reached about thirty feet, it began to bulk up, growing big and strong and wide rather than too tall.  In a very few years, much of the front of the house was shaded and comfortable in the afternoon; our cooling bills went down, and we were able to enjoy  evenings in the living room without sweat on our brows.  Dog walkers liked to stop under our tree for a rest, as did human walkers and runners.  My sprites had lemonade and cookie sales under the tree.   We had an unreasonably large number of Covid gatherings in the shade of our elm, so welcoming and calming. Elms are also food trees for all kinds of birds, squirrels, and bees.  Important, especially, for birds in the winter who love the tiny persistant seeds.  It was the  tree for entertainment for squirrels and birds alike. The tree was such a joy for me, every single day.  And in the blink of an eye, it went into a slow motion collapse in front of my eyes, splitting into three main parts. Additionally, towels can become contaminated with fecal matter, urine, and other bodily fluids, making them a potential source of infection if not washed regularly. How Often Should You Change Your Towels? Most experts recommend changing bath towels every three to four uses or every week, whichever comes first. For instance, if you live in a humid environment, you may need to change your towels more frequently to prevent mold and mildew growth. When to Replace Your Towels Aside from changing your towels regularly, it's also important to know when it's time to replace them. Towels have a bad smell that can't be washed out If your towels have a persistent odor, it's a sign that bacteria have taken hold and it's time to get rid of them. Towel color is fading If your towels are starting to fade, it's a sign that they've been washed too many times and are losing their effectiveness. Towels are thinning or fraying If your towels are thinning or fraying, it's a sign that they're reaching the end of their useful life and it's time to invest in some new ones. In conclusion, maintaining good hygiene starts with clean towels. title: Mistakes (boo boos) of the past week | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "publickman", "author_name": "Lars", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/publickman", "date": "2023-03-04", "text": "On Wednesday (I think), I decided to open up one of the cans of 6-in-One tomatoes that I had bought last year to make some marinara sauce.  I had ordered six cans of tomatoes at once, thinking that they would be 28 oz cans, but they turned out to be 105 oz (6 pounds, 9 ounces) cans, and so they each contain a bit over 13 cups of tomatoes each!  When I open one of these cans, I put most of the contents in the freezer, if possible. However, this week, I decided to try storing about 8 cups in jars that hold about 4 cups each, and I put some olive oil at the top to help seal the tomatoes from air and then vacuum sealed the jars.  Then I stored the two jars in the refrigerator in the garage, and I will find out later how this works out.  If it does not, I will not be that upset because these cans of tomatoes cost about the same price as the 28 oz cans, which is why I got confused when I ordered them. I used the remaining 5.5 cups of tomatoes to make the marinara sauce, and I decided to see how it would work in the pressure cooker.  First I saut\u00e9ed a large onion in some butter for a few minutes and then added 2-1/2 chopped toasted chiles de \u00e1rbol, some chopped red bell pepper, followed by minced garlic plus some thyme.  I let the garlic and thyme saut\u00e9 for only a minute or two before adding the tomatoes.  Then I added dried oregano, some San Giovese wine, a small amount of salt, and about a teaspoon of coconut sugar and brought the contents to a simmer. At this point, I put the lid on the pressure cooker and put the pan on my portable induction burner, and set that to cook at 212\u00b0 for 8 minutes.  I think this must have been too long because I started to notice a scorched smell coming from the pan, and so I shook the pan a bit and turned it off. I noticed that I should not have shaken the pan because some of the scorched tomato came to the top, but it was not too severe, but I was afraid to stir the pan because I expected it to be burned at the bottom, which was the case. I poured the sauce into an 8 cup Pyrex measuring cup (which I had been using for transferring the 8 cups of uncooked tomatoes into jars), and I stopped pouring when I got near the bottom and could see the burned portion.  I discarded the bottom layer that seemed to be scorched (since I had massive quantity anyway), and I tasted the sauce in the Pyrex.  It did not really taste burned but rather tasted more like fire roasted tomatoes, and so I decided that it was okay.  However, the chilies that I added must have been especially potent, as it was a bit hotter than I really wanted. I used the sauce on some fettuccine that I had cooked earlier for some pesto sauce that I had made, but I had made too much fettuccine, which is why it was leftover. First, I had made fresh fettuccine, using two eggs, one cup flour, and 1/4 teaspoon salt.  This made what appeared to me as three servings, and so I held back about a third of the pasta.  The next day I boiled some dried fettuccine, to use up the leftover pesto sauce, and the box of dried fettuccine had 8 ounces left, but I only wanted 5 ounces, which is what I normally cook for the two of us.  However, I decided that 3 ounces was not worth saving by itself, and so I cooked that also and held back one third of the cooked pasta.  Later, I added that to the leftover fresh pasta, and that seemed enough for two servings. This is getting long, and so I will continue in another post.", "images": []}

title: When to replace Hardie Board Siding ? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "takingthedayoff", "author_name": "takingthedayoff", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/takingthedayoff", "date": "2023-03-04", "text": "Our \u201cnew\u201d house was built in 1994 - with Hardie Board siding (before their very specific install instructions) and Milgard vinyl windows - so everything was very good in 1994 but is past it\u2019s lifespan now. With the exception of the wood edge trim, the Hardie is in fairly decent looking condition except for two problem areas with paint peeling - next to vent hood exhaust and above AC unit. The house needs some serious caulking around the windows ( siding installed before z flashing was required) as the state of the current caulk is allowing water to cause problems - not sure how long that\u2019s been going on - probably a while. The windows need to be replaced - several are foggy & don\u2019t shut well anymore. The caulk around the glazing is oozing out and the low e coating seems to be doing nothing at this point. We got a quote for $30k to replace the windows with exactly what\u2019s there now\u2026 25 windows - many very large. They would have to cut the siding and add trim (none currently) around the windows to do so. We also got quotes for painting the exterior $10k and $20k - I suspect a fair price is more like $15k. We could also just get the vinyl windows reglazed and replace the glass where needed for 1/2 the price. Some windows are probably too large for someone to want to touch so we\u2019d be stuck with those. We could remove and replace the bad portions of the siding and get everything painted. We get a lot of direct sun and sideways rain - suspect a paint job won\u2019t last 10 years no matter how good. I\u2019m wondering if we should caulk the windows and wait\u2026 save up to replace all of the siding at the same time. Based on the water issues I don\u2019t feel good about the house wrap / window flashing. Maybe we could also evict the attic flies who hibernate under the siding on the west side. I\u2019m also not a fan of the way the lap siding and shingles were combined on the exterior - the house is awkwardly shaped and they made it look worse. Does the prefinished Hardie with the 15 year color warranty make it worth it (added bonus of not having painters around for a while)? Is it insane to think about replacing the siding if only some of it is begging to be replaced? Does replacing the windows at the same time offer cost efficiencies? title: Madame Isaac in the garden today in Austin | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bob-atchisonpallasarthagiasophia", "author_name": "Bob Atchison - Pallasart - Hagia Sophia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bob-atchisonpallasarthagiasophia", "date": "2023-03-04", "text": "Beautiful, huge and fragrant on March 4th in Austin, Texas.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b6a23e250403b76c_5167-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bob-atchisonpallasarthagiasophia", "author_name": "Bob Atchison - Pallasart - Hagia Sophia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bob-atchisonpallasarthagiasophia", "date": "2023-03-05", "text": "Why do Bourbon roses do well in Austin? They were discovered on the \u00cele  Bourbon - now called R\u00e9union -  off the coast of Madagascar in the  Indian Ocean growing wild and free in the tropical heat. No one knows  for sure, since there are no records of how they were bred, it might  have been a natural cross-breeding, perhaps the result of a cross  between the old European rose, Autumn Damask, and the 'Old Blush' China  rose, both of which were frequently used as hedging materials on the  island. Hedges on the island were usually planted in two rows of these  roses. The fact that the Bourbon rose occurred naturally and flourished  on its own without human intervention meant it had been tried and proven  through natural selection by Mother Nature herself, which gave it  toughness and vigor.   Bourbons get their repeat bloom from their china  heritage and their big flowers and scent from the Damask.  Bourbon roses  are generally tough plants and can take the heat and sun, which made  them successful hedge plantings.  Bourbons can grow big, thick and tough  canes, many have thorns, which can be woven into natural fences.  The  Portuguese arrived on \u00cele Bourbon in the early 16th century. They could  have brought Damask roses there from Europe and other roses from China  and Japan.   They flower repeatedly on vigorous, frequently  semi-climbing shrubs with glossy foliage and purple-tinted canes. The  French arrived in the 1660's. \"Bourbon\" comes from the name of the royal  house of France. Breon, a botanical traveler for the French Government,  arrived on the island in 1817 and was curator of the Botanical and  Naturalization garden there.  A man named Perichon in San Benoist, in  planting a hedge found in his young plants one that was very different  from the others in its shoots and foliage, which was purple when new and  evergreen with huge rough leaves.  Breon grew many examples of this  rose and sent both seeds and plants to Henri Antoine Jacques, gardener  at the Chateaux de Neuilly, estate of the Duc d' Orleans, - who later  became King of France - near Paris, France, who distributed the rose to  all of the top rose cultivars in France.  At that point the rose was  commonly called Bourbon Jacques.  In the spring of 1821 it became a model for the famous rose painter, Redoute as Rosier de Bourbon. Seeds from this rose were very fertile and vigorous, it took a couple  of years of breeding to perfect the flowers and the plant was introduced  commercially as cuttings in 1821.  Bourbon roses were not a success in  England at the time, English gardeners thought the rose was not  well-mannered, course, with big flowers and a scent was too strong and  bold.   My favorite Bourbons are Madame Isaac Pereire from 1881 and Madame Ernst Calvat,  a natural sport - or mutation - of Madame Isaac discovered in 1888.   Madame Isaac was bred by by Armand Gar\u00e7on and introduced in France by  Margottin P\u00e8re & Fils of Paris who were horticulturists and plant  retailers.  Madame Isaac is a big plant that can grow canes up to 12  feet in length - it is often grown as a climbing rose and is an  effective rose for an arch or pergola. The leaves are large and the  rose-madder colored deep purple flowers are among the biggest to be  found in roses.  They are 5-6 inches, very full with more than 40  petals, cupped with a quartered bloom form - very cabbagey!  The scent  is very strong - perhaps the strongest deep rose perfume to be found -  deep, heavy Damask with raspberry which adds sweetness is the way to  describe it.  The scent can last all day.  The branches are covered with  dozens of flowers (hundreds on a mature plant) and in my garden the  scent carries across the street.  Madame Isaac blooms in waves, a huge  long one in spring of 45 days followed by lesser waves of flowers in  late summer and Fall.  I have even had flowers on Madame Isaac in  December and January if there is no frost.  It's a good cut rose in  informal, old rose arrangements.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7df257b20404ee0e_4686-w240-h238-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/318237490404eda5_4581-w240-h238-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

main_question: {"author_id": "susan-walter95", "author_name": "Susan Walter", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/susan-walter95", "date": "2023-03-05", "text": "A hummingbird began building a nest on the cord of lights on covered patio.  She was there for 3-4 days, left for another 3-4 days and then returned.  Tne nest now appears to have partially disconnected from the wire--  was hanging vertical now looks horizontal.  She has returned to the feeder but not to the nest. We had a nest last year on lights and baby successfully hatched.  Wondering if they ever build 'unsuccessful' nests?  The nest is also in a high traffic area--  do we need to steer clear if she returns?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gyr-falcon", "author_name": "gyr_falcon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gyr-falcon", "date": "2023-04-08", "text": "It doesn't sound as if the nest is very secure, so it may have been abandoned for that reason. Activity tolerance varies a lot--I have seen many a nest in busy plant nurseries, or next to the sidewalk of active businesses. Some mother hummers are calm, and others dive at everyone that walks by. Females that have had a successful nest season will often return to the same general, or even the exact, location the following year. This might be the same female that nested on your lights last year. If so, and if the two locations are not very different activity-wise, perhaps she is already comfortable with the amount of activity in that area. If eggs were not yet laid, it is possible she will build another nest nearby. It isn't unusual for the bird to leave and return for stretches at a time during construction and egg laying.", "images": []}}

I've got like 40 canes of rootstock just chilling in water before i even plant them to root, but I've got some great budwood that I would much like to use now. I know this budwood canes just won't root on their own no matter what method or incantation I attempt, so that's not an option. Can it be done? Is it much too difficult?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "roseseek", "author_name": "roseseek", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roseseek", "date": "2024-10-25", "text": "Sequoia Nursery grafted and rooted mini standards under mist for decades. The trick is using mist so the bud is kept moist until it knits with the stock so it doesn't dry out. The scion requires moisture either from being knitted to the stock or from being bathed by external moisture until the two pieces grow together. An unrooted stock is not flowing sap as there are no roots to absorb the water to be pushed up to the scion. Unless the process is conducted under pretty much 100% humidity so there is no possibility of the two pieces drying out before they knit together, I don't know how else it could be done successfully. Sequoia used a 3# coffee can with holes punched around the base about an inch from the bottom. Bundles of unrooted long whips with minis grafted to their tops were inserted into the can and placed under mist on a outdoor mist table which received strong, filtered light through the surrounding trees. During their hot weather, the bottoms of the whips remained in about an inch of water while the rest of the cuttings were maintained bathed in a mist of water which went off periodically. The strong light helped all the green parts to continue producing chlorophyll, feeding them until they grew roots and knitted together, at which point they were individually potted and replaced under less mist to gradually harden off and moved out into the sales area.", "images": []}}

There are several factors to consider before purchasing an area rug for a queen bed. TYPE OF BEDFRAME Not all bed frames are created equally. Everything from texture, style, color, and visibility are critical factors in choosing an area rug for a queen bedroom set. For frames that sit lower on the ground, a bright pop of color can work against the room and swallow up the furniture. A subtle or pastel area rug may disappear and feel unnecessary for large poster bed frames, lending a sense of chaos or insignificance. BEDROOM FURNITURE Are you building the design in this bedroom around the bedframe? Is the furniture modern, and do you want the rug to help with traditional values, or is it meant to encourage a free spirit? ROOM SIZE The room size will ultimately guide the purchase of the area rug. For queen beds, area rugs under 4\u00d76 will neither add to space nor be visible. Area rugs are traditionally placed under the bed, and certain rooms may even feel smaller after adding an area rug. THE RANGE OF RUG SIZES FOR QUEEN BEDS Choosing the right rug size for queen beds is a simple equation.Bedrooms, on average, are 9.6 x 10 square feet. A queen bed is, on average, 60 inches x 80 inches long. The right area rug for your space should extend 12-18 inches from the frame and leave room for walkability without being touched. However, using two 4\u00d76 rugs is slightly larger than a 9\u00d712 rug and will take up more space or be challenging to ensure symmetry. 5X7FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN A 5\u00d77 area rug is the smallest we recommend and is great for smaller bedrooms or guest rooms. Due to the length, we caution using dual nightstands or organizing furniture flushed to a wall rather than in the middle of the space. 5X8FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN If choosing to use this size of an area rug, place it away from the back wall and instead lay the rug starting from the nightstands. The 6\u00d79 measurement is also ideal for wider bed frames and will provide soft carpeting on three sides of the bed frame. 7X10FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN For larger master bedrooms, a 7\u00d710 area rug will fit beautifully under any bedframe. This size of fabric has the potential to add depth and creativity to a space while not prohibiting other furniture pieces from standing out or blending into the design vision. 8X10FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN The last two area rug sizes will highlight bigger-than-average rooms. Standard bedroom sizes are 11\u00d712, but for these last two area rug sizes to work, the bedroom should be a minimum of 12\u00d712 or even 14\u00d715. 9X12FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN You have two options for laying the rug for either 8\u00d710 or 9\u00d712 area rugs under queen frames. Option one would be to lay the rug under both nightstands and the bed or option two would position the rug about a quarter of the way down from the head of the bed. Option two placement works best with more extended bed frames, including California or Olympia queen frames, or with furniture at the foot of your bed. TRADITIONAL OR CONTEMPORARY: THE TSAR APPROACH While these measurements are best with square and rectangle area rugs, don\u2019t be discouraged from putting circular area rugs in bedrooms. With smaller bedrooms, a circular rug can help to isolate space and give purpose or meaning. For bedrooms that are 10\u00d712, a round rug fits nicely next to the bed frames. For larger bed frames, you can put the area rug at the end of the frame as a creative fringe and injection of personality. Green Giant arborvitaes are very hardy, not expensive even in larger sizes and can put on as much as 3 feet of growth a year. title: Power out for days | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kathleen-smith6227819", "author_name": "Kathsgrdn", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kathleen-smith6227819", "date": "2023-03-06", "text": "From about Friday afternoon till about an hour ago.  It has been miserably cold especially at night, a two comforter night  (  :  Today it was in the low 70s and I thought tonight wouldn't be so bad but then the power came back on.  High winds.  Lot of damaged trees and buidlings in the state.  I lost at least 3 shingles on my outbuidling.  I can't see the backside so not sure if that is all that's missing.  Now will have to find someone to repair that.  I think there were four or five deaths, so sad, it was a scary storm.  The business next to where my daughter was working had their roof collapse.  Roof collapsed here on Main street too, at a sandwich shop me and a friend had just eaten at the day before. I was able to shower on Saturday, the water was still almost hot.  The next day I skipped bathing.  This morning was going to take a sponge bath but the air temperature was just too cold and I took a friend's invitation from Saturday to go shower at her house.  She also let me store all my freezer food.  I lost the stuff in the fridge.  Thank goodness there wasn't alot in there. For the entire time I thought, \"I'm getting a generator\" but then I looked at the cost of them, cost of installation and then cost of adding a fuel source and I don't know if I want to spend that much money.   I'm pretty sure there are gas lines in the neighborhood and thought I may go that way.  Several of my neighbors have them, they're very loud lol. I bought a Coleman stove and teapot to boil water for coffee and warm up some canned foods.  I had to buy the canned foods too since I didn't have any in my cupboard.  I bought a little lantern so I could read since there wasn't much to do.  I never did read though and would go to bed about 8:00 pm.  I had all those things for camping but gave them to my son years ago.  Now I can take them all on my trip to Oregon and use them in case this happens again.  I'm just glad it's over now.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mamiller040256", "author_name": "M Miller", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mamiller040256", "date": "2023-03-07", "text": "These \"Pros\" on this forum regularly advise finding an \"independent kitchen designer\".  So much of the comments here are for if you lived in an ideal world, or if you live in a HCOL area with plenty of design showrooms catering to $100k+ kitchens, or if Architectural Digest was a real place where everyone employs multiple designers returning their calls instantly.  Another thing that is true for every profession, whether it is kitchen design, doctors, lawyers, teachers, anything, is that there are good ones and bad ones, and just cause you have a KD certification does not mean you will be good. The budget issues though are real.  I would increase to $60k which will get you a nice middle-of-the-road kitchen for the work you described, and if you are careful about your choices of materials. Most \"independent kitchen designers\" do not work on the kind of kitchen the OP is talking about.  Furthermore, most kitchen designers are not independent, but work within a kitchen showroom or cabinet showroom.  Depending on where you are located, it can be difficult to drum up enough business independently as a kitchen designer, so most are aligned with a showroom.  While it could happen that a kitchen showroom could pad the budget by designing cabinets and extras you don't need, the good ones will not.  They want repeat business, they want word-of-mouth business, and they don't want negative reviews online.  And oh yeah, the good ones are ethical. If you feel your design is padded, you can always come on this forum and get opinions on whether it is. What you need to do is visit several kitchen showrooms and/or look at cabinet lines you like, and find their local showrooms, then sit down with people there, and get a feel for which ones you \"gel\" with, and also which ones are willing to help you given your budget.  So, you've got some homework and legwork to do.  It is only after that legwork and homework that you can choose which designer you want to go with, and yes, pay them a design fee. I went to a cabinet showroom (that would be \"oh no!\" according to this forum), and got a wonderful kitchen design from their representative.  But I came armed with rough measurements of my kitchen, what look I wanted (photos from magazines and online), what type of appliances I wanted (e.g., a range vs separate cooktop/wall ovens), and most of all, my budget.  If you expect to be spoon-fed every detail of your kitchen, that would be a mistake.  You need to come armed with some basis to go by, or they will politely tell you they can't help you, or even will ghost you. I would not go to a Home Depot or any big box store though.  Anyway, we went over the kitchen plans several times, they came to the house and measured, and were very on top of the cabinet shipping and delivery. title: Wool rugs FAQS (Frequently Asked Questions) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tsar-carpets-pfvwau-pf~1011472793", "author_name": "TSAR Carpets", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/carpet-dealers/tsar-carpets-pfvwau-pf~1011472793", "date": "2023-03-07", "text": "Wool rugs are best known for their durability and aesthetic appeal. They are also more versatile and easy to maintain; hence most owners will choose a wool rug over synthetic fiber rugs like acrylic polyester and nylon. Check out our FAQs section to learn more about woolen rugs, their features, pros, cons, and everything in between. Wool as a material is one of the common natural fibers used to make carpets and area rugs. Our Wool rugs in Melbourne are durable and flexible for every space. Whether you need a small and soft wool rug for your bedroom or a larger, water and stain-resistant design for high-traffic areas, we have got you covered. All the rugs in our custom Melbourne rug shop meet the highest design quality, and you\u2019ll surely find the best design to suit your unique needs. Check out our wool rug FAQs below to help guide your decision-making. What are wool rugs? Wool rugs are natural handwoven fibers that can be customized to suit different floors and environments. They are resilient to the forces of wear and tear and are the most sought-after type of rugs on the market. Are wool rugs worth the money? Yes. Not only are wool rugs natural and durable, but they also enhance the aesthetic appeal of your space. How can you know if a rug is woolen? Remove one fiber from the rug and hold it using a paper clip. Use a lighter or matchbox to burn the fiber, then check how it burns. If the fiber burns slowly with an orange glow and without any smoke, then it\u2019s wool. It should also smell like burnt hair. What are the main benefits of a wool rug? Wool rugs are hypoallergenic, making them suitable for everyone in the family, including pets. They are also sustainable, long-lasting, and low maintenance. Are wool rugs expensive? Due to their reliability and aesthetics, wool rugs are costly compared to nylon and other synthetic rugs. How long do wool rugs last? With proper care & maintenance, a wool rug can last anywhere from 30 to 50 years. On the other hand, synthetic rugs will only last 3 to 5 years. What makes a rug luxurious? The material used to make the rug, such as wool fibers, and the design often make some rugs more admirable than others. Check out our Luxury Melbourne Rug page for different designs of high-end wool rugs. Are wool rugs itchy? Not necessarily. Wool rugs with shorter and rough fibers can irritate the skin as they rub against it. However, those with longer and softer fibers are very comfortable. What are the pros and cons of wool rugs? Some of the key benefits of wool rugs are durability, color retention, sustainability, and versatility. One of the biggest downsides is the high upfront cost. Does wool fade in sunlight? If you expose your wool rug to sunlight for an extended period, it will fade with time. Do wool rugs smell? Yes, but under certain circumstances. The wool rug will develop an unpleasant smell if it has some mold or mildew build-up. Do wool rugs get softer over time? Yes. Wool rugs will often feel softer with time, making them even more comfortable. Does wool catch fire? Unlike synthetic rugs, wool is flame and fire-resistant. Similarly, they do not melt or stick to the skin when they burn. This makes them a great option for areas with high risks of fire incidents. Are all wool rugs the same? No. Wool rugs vary in quality, thickness, size, and design. The best wool rug for you will depend on your unique needs. Browse through our Rug Shop Melbourne collection to find the best wool rug that suits your taste and budget. Does wool last longer than cotton? Both wool and cotton are more durable than synthetics. However, wool last slightly longer than cotton, provided both are well taken care of. Do wool rugs stain easily? No. Often, wool rugs will repel stains unless they are exposed to stains frequently or for longer periods. They are also easy to clean; hence stains can be removed more effectively. Does wool attract mold and mildew? Wool rugs have fibers that allow moisture to pass through efficiently. This creates a less-than-ideal environment for mildew and mold growth. However, this isn\u2019t to say that wool rugs are mold or mildew-resistant. Proper care and maintenance are still crucial. Do wool rugs ever stop shedding? Your wool rug may shade in the first few months after purchase, but this will stop after a couple more months of continuous use. Vacuuming your rug properly will help stop shedding. Does wool have elasticity? Wool is naturally elastic; hence it can stretch and shrink. The extent of this elasticity depends on the quality of the fiber, the thickness, and the overall design. Can you hose down a wool rug? During a deep cleaning exercise, yes; otherwise, you shouldn\u2019t wet the entirety of your wool rug. This is because you won\u2019t be able to dry it fast enough, and this can cause mold and mildew issues. How can you know if a rug is of good quality? You can tell the quality of a rug by looking at the number of knots per square inch. The higher/more the number of knots, the better the quality. Other factors to consider are the feel and softness of the fibers, how detailed the patterns are, and how rich the color is. Do dogs like wool? Pets love woolen rugs, thanks to the soft and comfortable feel. This also means you\u2019ll need to regularly vacuum your rug to get rid of dog hairs and dander. Are vegans against wool? By definition, vegans are generally against exploiting animals for food, clothing, cosmetics, etc. This means wool isn\u2019t vegan; however, we can\u2019t confirm whether most vegans are against wool. Is wool water resistant? Yes, but up to some extent. A high-quality wool rug repels moisture droplets. It can also absorb up to one-third of its weight in moisture without feeling wet. Is wool rough or smooth? Wool, like cotton, has air spaces, which makes them rough to touch. They also have uneven surfaces, unlike nylon or silk, made of long and plain fabrics. Are wool rugs difficult to take care of? No. If you use the right cleaning components and techniques, caring for wool rugs is relatively easy. You can maintain a wool rug with frequent vacuuming, spot cleaning, and deep cleaning. Can you use vinegar on a wool rug? Yes. Vinegar is great for removing dirt and oil from your stained wool rug. You\u2019ll need to add one cup of vinegar to two cups of water, then apply it to the stained parts while scrubbing it with an old toothbrush or another soft scrubbing element. Can you use/put baking soda on a wool rug? Baking soda is often used as a DIY cleaning technique for wool rugs. And while the entire process can be tedious, it\u2019s a great alternative if you don\u2019t want to use vinegar or detergents. How do you get rid of the musty smell in wool? Use a gentle detergent to wash the woolen rug, then add two tablespoons of white vinegar to the water used for a final rinse. Let the rug fully dry. If the smell persists, wash it again with vinegar until the smell disappears. Do not use harsh/strong detergents or chlorine bleach as they will damage the wool fibers. Can you vacuum a wool rug? Yes. You should vacuum your wool rug at least once every week. Always use a vacuum without a beater bar, as this can cause or expedite shedding problems. How do you clean urine in a wool rug? Use water and vinegar to clean the affected areas. You can also try baking soda, and mild liquid soap. Be sure to mix these ingredients in reasonable, preferably equal proportions.", "images": []}

For dairy I used sour cream plus an additional tablespoon and a half, as the mixture needed more liquid.  The eggs were warmed in hot water to room temp, which always IME produces a better result in baked goods. Anyway, a great result and I am going to make these for next week\u2019s luncheon.  They are rich and flavorful and the sharpness of that tomato relish will be a perfect accompaniment.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ded2f2dc0407732b_9957-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Why does my Kohler engine smoke | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-998462042", "author_name": "HU-998462042", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-998462042", "date": "2023-03-07", "text": "I have a Cub Cadet mower with a Kohler Courage 23 HP engine and every time I do a cold start, it smokes.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-128654167", "author_name": "Travis Johnson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-128654167", "date": "2023-03-10", "text": "We really do not have enough information to give you a good answer. If it is brand new it might be because it is still \"breaking in\" the engine which is where everything is new and kind of needs to seat in. That can take a bit of time depending on the oil that is in it. If It is kind-of-new, then it might be because of not breaking in the new engine correctly. If the engine is run at a set RPM all the time, then it can wet-stack, and smoke or pump oil out of the exhaust. If its been an engine you have been running forever, then it could have a broken ring, or worn rings. Or it could be as simple as, being an air cooled engine, it has not got up to temperature yet, the cylinder and piston have not expanded quite enough to give a good seal against the oil rings. But as soon as it comes up to proper temperature, it seals and stops smoking.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-998462042", "author_name": "HU-998462042", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-998462042", "date": "2023-03-11", "text": "The motor has about 450-500 hours and it only smokes when I first start it.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "1saxman", "author_name": "1saxman", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/1saxman", "date": "2023-03-11", "text": "Black smoke, blue smoke or white smoke (not talking about some possible water vapor at first in cold weather)? If it's 'blue/black', it is the result of a rich condition where the choke is too closed and too much fuel is in the cylinders. This 'washes down' engine oil in the cylinder and burns it. Blue smoke is just oil. White smoke is also oil but usually coming in at the valve seals. Your engine might just be wearing out early for any number of reasons. Black smoke is too rich but not washing down oil YET! Fix that choke now and avoid irreversible damage.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "webuser-866646995", "author_name": "\u53f8\u5f92\u4e8c\u4eba", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-866646995", "date": "2023-03-20", "text": "ok", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "sapphire131", "author_name": "SEA SEA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sapphire131", "date": "2023-03-08", "text": "John Brady, Not beaglenc here. In my experience, yes, both of those powders can fade colors over time, unless it is a truly colorfast fabric. I weigh the risk vs benefit in using those powders. Ex: is this navy blue cotton men's dress shirt so dirty, greasy or smelly that shortening it's usable life is needed by using a higher wash temp and a quality powder detergent such as Tide? Keep in mind that the definition of warm and hot in regards to washing machines varies greatly, depending on the machine and it's temperature settings. In some machines, warm is defined as 85F. In others, warm is 120F, whereas, in yet other machines, hot is defined as 100-110F. This makes it challenging to determine what warm or hot means when reading about other's laundry practices and their eventual outcomes. Warmer wash temps and powder detergent can equal more fading in colors. In answer to your question about Tide Orginal vs Tide F&G powders, I find that Tide Original cleans very well, checking the boxes one wants taken care of. Tide F&G powder does a good job too--removes many stains in day to day regular laundry. You likely know lots of people use it for cloth diapers with success, and I can't think of a higher demand laundry situation than cloth diapers. Where we, in this household can run into trouble is when I lean heavily on Tide F&G powder and then others come in after me and are using liquid detergent often. We can get a build up of funk that the Tide F&G can't remove in this situation. I suspect this is because it contains less oxygen bleach and does not have an activator. In your opening paragraph, imo, that is a fine laundry practice. I don't use powder Cheer too much anymore because finding it around here has become too difficult. But I did have good outcomes with Cheer powder. It just seems to be too hard to obtain and I've moved on. I use Tide w/Bleach powder on whites and lights only. I've read of others who use it consitantly on all of their laundry in warm water and don't complain of fading. I would have fading of colors with it, but they say they don't experience that. This would be my advice: 1) figure out how much money you have available for the project. 2) figure out why you want raised beds. it could be aesthetics, physical situation like bad back or arthritis, or as your case sounds like you perceive you have a soil problem. 3) you sound like you are just starting (yeah- exciting!) so take some photos of your problem and at a quart bag of soil to at least 2 local and well reputed garden center (not a place like Lowes, etc but a true local garden center) and see what they think specifically about your soil. title: How to choose the right rug and carpet? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tsar-carpets-pfvwau-pf~1011472793", "author_name": "TSAR Carpets", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/carpet-dealers/tsar-carpets-pfvwau-pf~1011472793", "date": "2023-03-08", "text": "Choosing the right carpet and rug can brighten a space and bring life to any area of your home. Check out this article for everything you need to know when picking the perfect carpet or rug HOW TO PICK A RUG There are lots of things to bear in mind when choosing the perfect rug for a room, from material to colour to placement to weave. It can all seem overwhelming when you first start looking through catalogues and websites! In this rug buying guide we will take you through each decision step by step so you can be sure you\u2019re making the right choice. WHICH ROOM? Different rooms need different kinds of rugs. You don\u2019t want to put a thick woollen rug in your hallway as it will hold onto every bit of dirt and mud, making it impossible to clean. High traffic areas such as hallways and kitchens are best suited to rugs that are hardwearing and easy to clean. You might want to consider rugs with dark patterns that can hide stains that you can\u2019t get out. Similarly, you shouldn\u2019t put a hardwearing and coarse rug in your bedroom as it will be uncomfortable under bare feet. Alternatively, you can put super comfortable, soft and high pile rugs in bedrooms and living rooms with lower footfall and in places where you won\u2019t have to worry so much about keeping them clean. SIZE AND SHAPE There\u2019s a saying in the rug industry: bigger is usually better. If you put a small rug on its own in a large space it will give the appearance that it\u2019s \u2018floating\u2019 in the middle of some place it shouldn\u2019t be. You either want your rug to go underneath and around all the furniture in your room or, if that\u2019s not possible, to go under the front feet or all the furniture in the room. Depending on the space you might need a square or rectangular rug to do that. Before you look at anything, when you\u2019re at home take a tape-measure and measure out the size you want your rug to be so you know what you\u2019re looking for before you leave! MATERIAL Now that you know which room your rug is going to go in and the size and shape you want it to be, you need to move on to what can seem like the most daunting part of the decision \u2013 the material. But don\u2019t worry, choosing the best material doesn\u2019t need to be overwhelming. ACRYLIC Acrylic is both cheap and easy to maintain. It doesn\u2019t shed any of its fibre, so it lasts a long time and you don\u2019t have to worry about losing half your rug every time you vacuum! It varies in quality from soft to coarse depending on how well it has been made, so if you\u2019re buying acrylic look for a rug with a high knot count. Acrylic is hard-wearing, which makes it perfect for entrance ways and hallways. Also, it dyes easily so you can get lots of interesting patterns and colours. Consider a statement rug in the entranceway of your home that really shows off your personality. NATURAL WOOL When you think about digging your toes into a nice thick rug, you\u2019re probably thinking about a wool rug. Wool is super soft, warm, easy to clean and heat resistant \u2013 making it perfect to have in front of a fire or beside your bed. It\u2019s also completely sustainable and biodegradable, because it\u2019s naturally farmed. However, all these things make it more expensive than other options, especially for felted wool. SILK There\u2019s a reason silk is associated with emperors, queens and Hollywood stars on the red carpet\u2026 It\u2019s because silk is probably the highest quality fabric in the world. All the hard work and creativity of humanity still hasn\u2019t been able to surpass this elegant, beautiful and natural material. The feel is soft and luxurious, and because it\u2019s completely natural it\u2019s much better for the environment than other materials. All these upsides do come with their own problems. It\u2019s delicate, meaning it can be easily torn and if you knock over a glass of red wine or black coffee, it can be easily stained. In addition, it\u2019s the most expensive material on this list. All this means this is not the rug to put in your entranceway. Consider a silk rug for your bedroom, or if you don\u2019t have kids or pets, perhaps your living-room. SILK \u2018LOOKALIKES\u2019 \u2013 KRISTAL AND TENCEL Kristal and Tencel are man-made fabrics designed to look and feel like silk, but are cheaper and easier to mass produce. Both feel great and are more durable and stain resistant than silk, as well as being easier to clean and care for. Tencel is generally the better quality and more expensive of the two options, but both should be only reserved for living-rooms and bedrooms. PLANT BASED MATERIALS (JUTE, SISAL, SEAGRASS) There seems to be an increasing number of rugs made out of vegan, plant based materials such as Jute, Sisal and Seagrass. They\u2019ve been used for hundreds of years, and although they went out of fashion in the 20th century they\u2019re coming back as, unlike plastic-based materials such as acrylic and nylon, they are vegan and 100% natural, with small carbon footprints. They are cheap and hard-wearing, but very coarse, so good if you want a natural material for a high footfall area like a hallway or entrance way, but not great for anywhere you might be walking around barefoot. They are generally easy to clean, however, Sisial requires a special dry cleaning kit if it gets wet. COTTON There\u2019s a very good chance you are wearing cotton right now \u2013 perhaps a soft cotton t-shirt or a nice warm cotton sweater. There\u2019s a reason we use cotton so much \u2013 it feels great, it\u2019s natural, cheap and easy to dye any colour you can think of. All this means it\u2019s a great option for a new rug, especially for living rooms and bedrooms where you want to feel it under your feet. The only real downside is that, just like your socks, a cotton rug can wear through faster than other materials so make sure you put it somewhere without too much footfall. CONSTRUCTION Rugs come either in \u2018High Pile\u2019 or \u2018Low Pile\u2019. High pile is a longer, thicker density option that is deep, comfortable and snug \u2013 think about digging your toes into a comfy rug on a cold night. But because it\u2019s thicker, it\u2019s more expensive and it\u2019s easy to get dirt and mess trapped between the fibres. High pile rugs are perfect to put in the living room or bedroom, anywhere that won\u2019t have dirty shoes walking back and forth. Low Pile is cheaper, with shorter fibres that aren\u2019t as comfortable under your feet but don\u2019t hold onto dirt like high pile rugs. They tend to be thin and hard-wearing compared to high pile rugs. They\u2019re great for high footfall areas and places that need to be regularly cleaned like hallways, entranceways and kitchens. PATTERN AND COLOUR What colour and pattern you have on your rug will depend on the material you choose. Some materials, like acrylic, take colours easily so the only limit to what you can have is your imagination. If you have a room without a lot of colour and energy you might want to consider a rug with bold patterns and bright colours to add energy to a room without being overwhelming. Alternatively, you can help to quieten a bright or busy room with a more plain rug in a simple colour. TIPS & TRICKS CHOOSING THE RIGHT CARPET Just like choosing the right rug, you have to think about three important things when choosing the perfect carpet: high pile or low pile; colours and patterns, and material. In this section of the guide we\u2019ll take you through room by room and tell you what to bear in mind when choosing your carpet. An important thing to think about is, do you have pets and will pets ever go in the room you are carpeting? Some carpets have \u2018looped weaves\u2019 which can catch on the claws of cats and small dogs and should therefore be avoided at all costs if you have pets (for their sake and yours). THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR KITCHEN It doesn\u2019t matter how clean and tidy a cook you are, sooner or later food will get dropped on your kitchen floor. So you might want to avoid carpet completely around the food preparation area. When buying carpet for any part of your kitchen, choose a carpet with a low pile as these are easier to clean. You might also want to consider a carpet with interesting colours and patterns that can hide any possible stains, and avoid completely pale carpets that easily show marks. Consider Nylon, Acrylic and plant-based materials for your kitchen as these are easy to clean and hard-wearing. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR STAIRS Stairs get a lot of traffic, all day everyday, so you want low pile and hard-wearing materials like Polypropylene, Nylon, Acrylic and plant-based that are easy to clean. The most important thing to bear in mind, is to avoid patterns on your stairs, as these confuse anyone walking up and down and might cause them to fall. Keep the carpet simple and easy to see the edges. If your stairs are made of good looking wood, consider a \u2018runner\u2019 down the centre of your stairs that shows off the wood on each side. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR LIVING ROOM There will be a lot less footfall in your living room and fewer people walking through with dirty shoes, so you can choose to have a thick, high pile carpet that will feel good under bare feet \u2013 consider cotton, wool, silk or one of the silk lookalikes. Because it will get less dirty than other rooms you can also choose to go for a light coloured carpet if you want. A cream or beige carpet can be a great way of lightening a room that\u2019s got dark furniture or walls. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR HALLWAY AND ENTRANCE WAY The hallway and entrances are probably the most difficult places in your house to choose the right carpet for. It\u2019s the first part of your house guests see, so you want to make a good impression and show off your excellent taste and style, but it\u2019s also the place that gets the most footfall and is most likely to get marked and stained. Because people don\u2019t spend a lot of time in these places, we would recommend practicality and ease of cleaning over picking the most impressive \u2013 consider a low pile carpet made from Nylon, Acrylic, or plant-based materials. These materials are easy to clean, hard-wearing and don\u2019t stain too easily. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR BEDROOM When you get out of bed in the morning you want to be able to push your toes into a warm and comfortable carpet that soothes your feet. That means the bedroom is the part of the house where you can choose the deepest, lushest and most comfortable carpet available. And, because the bedroom gets much less footfall than other rooms, you don\u2019t have to worry too much about wearing through the material, so whenever possible, choose a high pile carpet and opt for cotton, wool, silk, Tencel or Kristal. When choosing a pattern or colour, go for something soothing \u2013 you probably don\u2019t want the last thing before you go to sleep to be a bright yellow carpet with orange stripes. If you're growing on a windowsill or near a source of daylight, that dictates your darkness schedule.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "beesneeds-pfvwus-pf~278115867", "author_name": "beesneeds", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/not-specified/beesneeds-pfvwus-pf~278115867", "date": "2023-03-12", "text": "In general, some seed that likes light for sprouting up like carrot and lettuce and tends to be surface sown or very lightly covered can appreaciate the light being on from sowing forward. Most seed that likes being more buried does not really need light till it starts popping out of the soil. But then you want to make sure it is getting light from that point on. Plants have circadian clocks- different species run on differing times of light and dark. When they are small seedlings it is usually beneficial for there to be longer times of light or no darkness. As they get older and start their own circadian rhythms some gardeners like to start giving hours of night or lights off to accomidate that. As they harden off it can be beneficial to adjust the night hours for plants akin to real night hours like we adjust their light from indoor to outdoor lighting during the day. In general, most plants are used to it being cooler at night than during the day. Seeds can benefit from additional warmth from a mat to sprout, but after that it is better to get the sproutlings off the heat. A couple few degree difference usually isn't a big deal for seedlings, it's the usual flux in a house. But a large temp drop or a lengthy one overnight can cause harm to many seedlings. Especially during the younger days of growth. I do my seedlings in a large south facing kitchen window that gets full sun, and I also run lights there. It stays temp stable on the warm side due to a basebord heater there. I use a couple of little four tier mini greenhouse cages for my shelving. I have a 24 hour on light for sproutlings. Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. title: Lights Flickering on New Build | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ashley-klesmit", "author_name": "Ashley K", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ashley-klesmit", "date": "2023-03-09", "text": "It\u2019s a long story, but I want to see if anyone has seen this before. If you like mysteries, this one is for you. We moved into our new build 10/31. We noticed that the light fixtures (not the can lights) would flicker for a couple seconds randomly. We didn\u2019t think there was a pattern to it. It wasn\u2019t when the AC or refrigerator kicked on. It was truly random and it happened at all times of the day. The electrician came out and tightened the screws on the breaker box. The flickering continued. He said it wasn\u2019t anything on his end. He said he had seen it once before where one LED bulb was causing multiple lights to flicker. We didn\u2019t think that was the issue for us, but we had every single bulb in the house replaced anyways. The flickering continued. We then had the electric company come out. They tightened the wires running to the house and replaced our brand new meter with another brand new meter. They ran a load test and confirmed that the power coming into the house was fine and said it wasn\u2019t an issue on their end. The flickering continued. We then talked to our neighbor (we had talked to one before who said he wasn\u2019t having any issues) and found out that he had been having the same problem since he moved in over a year ago. He had a different builder & different electrician, so we then knew it wasn\u2019t an issue with our electrical work. We had the electric company come back out, and they installed a recorder on our meter to see if they could catch any anomalies. We started tracking when the flickering would happen, and we noticed it happens almost every 15 minutes on the 30 second mark and it happens at the same time every day. It got to the point where we\u2019d look at the clock and could count down to when it would happen. It happens on every fixture that\u2019s on at the time. Our neighbor did the same thing, and his lights flicker at the exact same time as ours. The electric company come back out again today to remove the recorder. We shared our findings with him, and he said that was super strange and that a transformer doesn\u2019t have any timed mechanism in it that would cause that. They\u2019re likely going to replace the transformer just to be certain. He said that he has seen once before where this was happening and it was because of a faulty refrigerator that was pulling power from the transformer and making lights flicker. He was confused though as to why ours is on such a set schedule. In that instance, the house was the only house on the transformer. I\u2019m going to propose that the electric company turns off electricity at each house for 15-20 minutes during the times that we\u2019ve for sure seen the flickering to see if possibly one house is causing the flickering. It isn\u2019t our house since the flickering was happening at our neighbors house before our house even started to be built. (If you\u2019ve made it this far, thank you!!) Basically, there are three houses on one transformer. Two of them are seeing the flickering issue. One of them used to see the flickering issue. We\u2019re trying to confirm with him if he still sees it. He was the first house built that\u2019s on this transformer. All houses were built about a year apart & had different builders. They\u2019re all less than three years old. We\u2019re desperate. Has anyone ever seen anything like this?!", "images": []}

Are you going to weed eat, edge, blow clippings and any other jobs involved cutting grass?  What if there is only a 3 foot fence gate to enter the back yard?  Expenses include prorating the value of your truck, trailer, mower, hand tools, gas, maintenance, insurance, taxes and the wife's rate of spending. Look at the job site to make a determination and not just based on the size of the lot.  I'll give you a few tips.  If you charge twice the going rate for cutting the grass you'll get half the number of clients, but make the same amount of money. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-474174520", "author_name": "Daniel", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-474174520", "date": "2023-03-10", "text": "Good morning Houzz! The trunk line chase comes down 18\" from the 9' drywalled ceilings.  There is room in the trunk line to install canless lights. On the other end of the room is a 7' wide by 9' tall stone electric/linear fireplace bump-out with TV mounted above.  The fireplace comes out 1' from the wall and is floor to ceiling. We have been going back and forth on recessed can light placement in the basement because of the trunk line.  We have a 22 x 15 living room on first floor with only four, 6\" dimable cans and have no problem with lighting at night.  4 lights is way below the minimum required when you plug in the dimensions on the all of the lighting calculators. There is no natural light in this room as the basement is totally underground.  A sectional couch would end up being positioned under the trunk line chase facing the fireplace. We've discussed 4-can placement - problem we see with that is if we put cans in the 5' wide chase, then we'd assume centering the remaining two cans in the 10' wide area and worry this won't look totally symmetrical. We've discussed 6-can placement - we worry about a can being right in front of the TV mounted above fireplace and having to worry about glare. Another option we thought about was split the width essentially into three and place a row of 2 or 3 cans every 5 feet.  That would either give us 9-cans or 8 if we remove the one directly closest to and centered on the fireplace. Pics below.  We would appreciate any feedback.
