title: Rubble Foundation Questions | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-676442229", "author_name": "HU-676442229", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-676442229", "date": "2023-03-25", "text": "Our house (circa 1880) has a rubble foundation, mostly in solid condition though the summer plans were to repoint anything needing attention. Clearing our first corner (inside) we noticed dirt and some water seepage in a couple spots at the base of the foundation where the slab had been poured. We figure this may have been a dirt floor with a slab poured later at the level of the bottom of the foundation, but no matter, our question is what we should do with the gaps were the stones don't dip below slab level to fill these voids where there is nothing but dirt? In our preliminary research (we're noobs here) we've discovered some discussions about hydraulic cement, mortar, and concrete. Does anyone have experience with this scenario and advice for us?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "sigrida", "author_name": "Sigrid", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sigrida", "date": "2023-03-25", "text": "We have a stone foundation, with a basement floor that may or may not have been poured much later.  We've had water seepage through the stones (not the mortar).  The solution was to get the water away from the foundation.  My (amateur) advice is: 1)  Pay a lot of attention to when and where the water comes in.  Go out and look on rainy days.  We discovered our problem after crawling under cobwebby porch in a downpour --- a miserable task, but very informative.  If you understand where the water is coming from, dealing with it is much easier. 2) Make sure you are keeping water away from your foundations.  That all your gutters and downspouts are in working order and the water discharges far enough from the foundation. You may find an easy and cheap solution to your problem.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "worthyfromgardenweb", "author_name": "worthy", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/worthyfromgardenweb", "date": "2023-03-25", "text": "Here's the full treatment from one of the leading building scientists in North America.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2023-03-26", "text": "It sounds like you are trying to fill some gaps (mortar joints) where there is no mortar. If any new mortar were to be combined with old mortar, then the type of mortar would need to be closer in it's lime content to be equivalent in moisture transmission qualities. If however you are removing dirt to fill in gaps, you can just use a hydraulic cement or 'N' type mortar. Concrete has larger aggregate and is not a good gap fill material. You will still get water leakage, but maybe not free-flowing.", "images": []}}

If that person sees  and reads this, SHAME ON YOU!!!  Who knows if it will flower in 6  weeks, on the next flush; it normally does not repeat well once it turns  hot, and we're already getting days in the low 90s here.  So we may see no flowers at all this season.  One of the  frustrating aspects of having a garden fully open to the public 24/7.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fb9290a5041f355f_6887-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Ideas to discourage Canadian Geese? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jackbe1", "author_name": "jackbe1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jackbe1", "date": "2023-03-26", "text": "My yard backs up to a small lake (perhaps 10 acres).  The Canadian geese come into my yard and defecate constantly.  Can you recommend any sprays that actually work? or other ideas to discourage the geese from foraging in my grass?  My dog is not at all interested in chasing the geese.  She only likes to chase cats.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~278115867", "author_name": "beesneeds", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~278115867", "date": "2023-03-28", "text": "A couple folks around here use huge inflatable swans in their ponds. They look like pool floats meant for a kid or maybe small adult? Put it on an anchor so it floats around \"On patrol\", but does not float away. They are fun :) And seem to work. We have live swans on our biggest pond, they for sure work. Once it gets up to small lake size, if the habitat can support both birds your mileage on a fake swan can go down if there are already live ones on the lake. I've heard of dead goose or gator decoys being used, but haven't seen them in action. How are you utilizing the edge of the pond? Geese prefer a gentle and open edge to a pond. Easy to walk on, see predators coming, and easy take-off space if needed. Messing with that can be a great way to keep them from wanting to stick around. Doing a bit of habitat modification can often do the trick. If you run a wire about 8 inches off the ground close to the waters edge that will stop them. It's their fence height, they are unlikely to duck under or hop over it. If you use flash tape on it, all the better. 12-18+ inches of fence, stacked rocks or wood, various planting and growths, and the like can block them. A solid line or fence is best, though you can break it up a bit into layering your stuff and creating switchback spots to walk through. Humans and dogs are fine with walking through switchbacks. Wild geese are not so fond of walking through what they can't see over- particularly if there are several geese together. They will do it, they just aren't fond of it and if there is easier beach access elsewhere on the lake, they will choose it first.  If you can put a stringer across the water a foot or so off from shore, they won't swim over it to walk up onto the shore. Stepping or walling your shore can be possible in some situations. It makes the waters edge not swim to walk accessable for birds. One of my smaller ponds is very deep with a natural step edge dropping in, it's surrounded by tall grasses. I've seen many places have retaining walls that come straight up out of the water- it's often for shoring or retaining, but also is very good at creating the step that geese don't want to use. If your geese are ealier spring stopovers. Letting your lawn get a bit shaggier in the fall and holding off a bit in the spring can make your lawn seem not so tasty or hospitable by comparison to neighbors lawns that get their last cuts later or start earlier. Spring geese love a fresh and verdant spring lawn. If your lawn is made up of sweeter or more tender grasses, growing more bitter and tougher grasses can help a bit. Especially if other lawns have tasty grass growing in them. If you are spring seeding your lawn, geese go after that too.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-03-27", "text": "There are so many experts on Maple staining here who have never actually touched a can of stain or finished Maple.  Including Creative Cabinets,  which is a fake business that Verbo created to lend credence to his posts. Unfortunately, I suspect your contractor is also someone who may not really understand the task at hand.  Soft Maple will get paper white after a single bleaching and hard Maple lightens almost as easily but will not usually get paper white.  The blotchiness of Maple is not as problematic with whitewashing stains, as whitewashing stains are often not penetrating stains. Here are some suggestions from someone who often whitens Maple.  What I use really depends on the piece  of wood I am using.  Maple can get \u201cdirty\u201d it can have lots of small pitch pockets that make it look like someone took a black marker and made dozens of small black marks on every door, or it can be really beautifully grained. Test the Minwax on some drawer backs and see what it looks like.  White stains are mostly going to sit on top of the wood like paint because wood doesn\u2019t love to drink in titanium oxide.  It may look fine. If I was finishing cabinets I would just paint it.  One of the easiest and most common ways to whitewash cabinets is with a toner coat.   You literally just go buy a white coating and the same clear coating and mix one part white to ten parts clear and spray it (play with the ratio to get it right).  You can also use a clear base and colorant.  If you are happy with the look after a single coat, then switch to clear, if not add another coat.  Any experienced sprayer should be able to spray a toner coat. Maple bleaches easily and beautifully.  I use a lye etcher and a 35% hydrogen peroxide bleach, but with Maple you can honestly get away with household bleach.  Tamar over at 3x3 customs has a bleaching test video\u2026I would argue that my results are slightly better than hers, but a bit more difficult.   There are plenty of videos on bleaching wood and it is not difficult. Finally, if you are concerned about your contractor\u2019s ability to achieve good results, which may be a fair assessment given that he only uses Minwax products, investigate Rubio Monocoat hard wax oils.  The village idiot could apply Rubio Monocoat and get flawless results.  Hard wax oils are a strong and durable finish that are also infinitely repairable.   If you get a stain, just sand it out and apply the hard wax oil again, you will not be able to find the repair.   However, over time hard wax oils get pulled into the wood and so every five years or so you have to add a coat of renewer.  This is simply wiping the cabinets down with the renewal oil.  Hard wax oils are not quite as durable as conversion varnish or 2k polys, but again, they are repairable unlike those. If your Maple is pulling pink, which they sometimes do, add a mint white precolor to the Rubio.  If staining or painting add a small shot of green colorant to the coating (test results first).  On the color wheel greens are opposite of reds and so they neutralize red colors. Good luck -\u2014", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-03-26", "text": "No. 'Columnaris' and 'Fastigiata' are two separate cultivars of European hornbeam. 'Fastigiata' is the most commonly encountered of the two and it is a faster growing and taller and wider selection than 'Columnaris'. In fact, there is not much very fastigiate about 'Fastigiata', as over time it grows into a very plump, gumdrop shaped tree as much as 30' wide. If you want the tree to remain skinny, look for 'Frans Fontaine'. All of the positive aspects of Fastigiata but with a 12-15' spread at most. Fastigiata will wind up about twice that width. Columnaris also develops at a slower rate than Fastigiata but no hornbeam grows very quickly anyway. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-03-27", "text": "The photos are from too far away to be able to determine what weeds you might be dealing with.....if in fact they are weeds and not just natural woodsy undergrowth. You could start now if you like but I'd be inclined to wait until all that bare woody stuff leafs out and you can see what you are actually dealing with. If you need to be rid of it, cut everything back almost to ground level and then paint (not spray) the exposed stems with a brush killer like triclopyr. Waiting until the plants are in active growth is also the best application time for any herbicides as well. You may need a couple of repeat applications to get complete removal. And manually remove whatever herbaceous weeds you come across as they appear. After a good rain or watering the area well will make them easier to pull or remove. title: Designing a wall mount kitchen faucet, feedback? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hzdeleted-71558385", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-71558385", "date": "2023-03-27", "text": "Hello Houzz, I want to share a project that I've been working on for a few years.  A bit of my insight came from reading these forums, so first I want to appreciate all the comments and helpful information you share here on these boards. My project is a wall mount kitchen faucet that has all the features of a conventional deck mount: Single mounting body, single lever handle, pull down hose, and gooseneck spout.  I finally got to the point where I have a functioning prototype and I'm pretty encouraged by the results. The idea came about when I lived in a house from the late 1940's that had a chrome wall mount unit above the sink.  I fell in love with the qualities of a wall mount faucet: Simple clean look, easy to wipe counter behind sink, gives faucet an independent feel as it isn't tied to the counter.  After extensive research I could not find a new wall mount unit that offered the features available on deck mounts.  Of course there are plenty of wall mount faucets, but they are pretty limited in their features, usually resorting to some goofy system for getting the job done (I'm thinking about those pull down sprayers that are suspended by a giant spring, aka - restaurant dishwasher faucet) I began this project by creating rough sketches on paper and making models out of clay and rigid foam, then I moved on to learning CAD to create models for photoshop renderings and got serious with graph paper.  I even shared those here about a year ago, and received a chilly response.  Once I had some plans, I learned that a local university had a Prototype Development Lab and I collaborated with them to produce a functional prototype based on my designs. The prototype is made out of brass.  I built a mock-up kitchen sink by pouring a concrete countertop, tiling the backsplash and installing a \"window ledge\" to show how a wall mount faucet is compatible with a window above the sink.  The photos show the results and I tested it with running water, but there are a few details that might come up as questions. 1) The design of the prototype exterior is very simple, we decided to focus on the inner workings rather than aesthetics, the style of the faucet could be taken in many directions as there is a lot of bulk taken up by the boxy shape that can be removed for an elegant design.  Please don't get hung up on how it currently looks, the goal was a proof of concept. 2) The faucet is installed from the front and access to the wall cavity is only necessary under the sink, no need to open the wall up unless there was a stud directly behind the faucet location. 3) There is no hard plumbing in the walls necessary.  Supply lines run from the faucet to shut off valves under the sink, which can be plumbed up through the floor into the cabinet.  This means that even though there are lines carrying water through the wall cavity, the PEX or Copper lines do not have to be run in the exterior walls. I consider this a significant step toward bringing wall mount faucets into use again, our technology has changed quite a bit since they were mainstream and I see a window of renewal for them.  I am open to any comments, critiques - whatever you want to throw out, and can answer any questions you might have.  Thanks for looking!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b7c25dd904212fd8_6539-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/63a2479304212fd9_6540-w500-h754-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0e8276ca04212fd9_6540-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/eb325e5604212fda_6540-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/bcc273a804212fdb_6540-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: 5 Techniques pour limiter l’entretien de son jardin | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "atelier-morliere-pfvwfr-pf~312614682", "author_name": "ATELIER MORLIERE", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/landscape-architects-and-landscape-designers/atelier-morliere-pfvwfr-pf~312614682", "date": "2023-03-27", "text": "Les jardins sont une source de beaut\u00e9 et de r\u00e9confort, mais entretenir  un jardin peut \u00eatre chronophage et fastidieux. Si vous \u00eates \u00e0 la  recherche de moyens de limiter l\u2019entretien de votre jardin sans  sacrifier la beaut\u00e9, voici 5 techniques efficaces :   1. Choisissez des plantes peu exigeantes Pour limiter le  temps et l\u2019effort n\u00e9cessaires \u00e0 l\u2019entretien de votre jardin, optez pour  des plantes qui n\u2019ont pas besoin d\u2019\u00eatre arros\u00e9es r\u00e9guli\u00e8rement ou  entretenues fr\u00e9quemment. Les plantes \u00e0 faible entretien sont  g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement les plus adapt\u00e9es \u00e0 un jardin car elles n\u00e9cessitent moins  de travail et de temps de votre part. 2. Utilisez du paillage. Le  paillage est une excellente fa\u00e7on de maintenir l\u2019humidit\u00e9 et de limiter  les mauvaises herbes. Il suffit de recouvrir le sol avec une couche de  mat\u00e9riau organique ou min\u00e9ral, pour une protection durable contre les  mauvaises herbes. De plus, le paillage ajoute de la couleur et de la  texture \u00e0 votre jardin. 3. Le choix des mat\u00e9riaux. Le  choix des mat\u00e9riaux ad\u00e9quats pour le jardin peut r\u00e9duire  consid\u00e9rablement l\u2019entretien. L\u2019utilisation de mat\u00e9riaux durables et  r\u00e9sistants peut pr\u00e9venir l\u2019usure et n\u00e9cessiter un entretien minimal. Le  bois, par exemple, est un mat\u00e9riau naturel qui selon son usage, son  essence et son profil aura un entretien limit\u00e9. Les pierres tels que les  pav\u00e9s, les ardoises, les pierres naturelles, les briques et les dalles  sont \u00e9galement tr\u00e8s durables et faciles \u00e0 entretenir. Le m\u00e9tal comme  l\u2019acier corten ou l\u2019aluminium peut avoir de nombreuses utilit\u00e9s au  jardin tout en \u00e9tant un produit tr\u00e8s durable et facile d\u2019entretien. 4. La r\u00e9gularit\u00e9 d\u2019intervention. Il  vaut mieux faire de petites interventions r\u00e9guli\u00e8res plut\u00f4t que des  interventions tr\u00e8s espac\u00e9es mais qui en font une tache fastidieuse en  temps et peuvent \u00eatre aussi lourd en \u00e9quipement et mat\u00e9riel. Chaque  zone du jardin va demander un entretien minimum, il est donc  int\u00e9ressant de programmer les interventions \u00e0 y faire ainsi que la  fr\u00e9quence que l\u2019on est pr\u00eat \u00e0 y passer.  Ainsi, ce qui est pour un  certain nombre de personnes une corv\u00e9e d\u2019entretien deviendra un bon  moment pass\u00e9 au jardin. 5. Bien concevoir son jardin. title: Climbers:  roots in the ground, head in the sky | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-03-27", "text": "A quality of climbing roses I've noticed is their ability to explode in growth once they're trained up to a position where they can grow horizontally.  We have 'La Mortola' in a terraced bed which is backed by a terrace wall topped with a railing.  I fooled with this rose for years, training it along the railing, watching it grow and die back, seeing with dismay the results when DH undid all my careful training and tried sending the whole rose into the massive bay laurel growing nearby.  It was all pretty unsatisfactory until DH built a pergola up on the terrace, one you could walk under, and I trained LM up the terrace wall and railing and further up onto the pergola top.  LM loves it.  The ascending canes are leggy and scraggly, but on the pergola, growing horizontally, the rose is a luxuriant mass of canes and foliage.  From its exalted position it has also sent a couple of canes into the bay laurel, and may be able to colonize it at last.  'La Mortola' can get huge, and it's as thorny a rose as I've ever encountered, so I hope that from now on I'll be largely able to leave it alone, forget about training it, and simply admire its glory. Other roses growing as climbers with support:  'Archduke Joseph', trained through the persimmon and onto the pergola, originally sole property of the wisteria, behind it.  AJ is a climber tout court, and a big one, an own root rose planted around 2004.  I put a photo of it on HMF.  'Mrs. B.R. Cant' is having a very good stab at climbing.  A grafted plant also put in the ground around 2004, it heads up the terrace wall and railing and up onto a pergola on the terrace, as well as into a volunteer flowering ash that seeded itself in the terrace wall.  Down in the shade garden 'Vanity' has worked itself into the pyracantha hedge that backs up its bed and is spreading impressively.  It's a leggy rose, but I think that if it were forced to climb to get to the light and given a structure, it would be pretty wonderful.  I'm looking forward to admiring this specimen once I've reduced the pyracantha hedge to some kind of order:  right now it's an unaesthetic mess. A number of the Pemberton Hybrid Musks would be great for this purpose.  My neighbors used to have an extremely beautiful 'Cornelia' growing on a northwest-facing wall, until they destroyed it through butchery and neglect, but while it was properly tended to, it was wonderful, and a big plant. title: Créer un massif de plantes, les erreurs à éviter ! | Houzz Forum

Assurez-vous de planter des plantes qui conviennent \u00e0 l\u2019exposition de  votre massif. 2 \u2013 Planter les  mauvaises plantes ensemble : \u00c9vitez de planter des plantes qui ont des  besoins diff\u00e9rents en termes de sol, d\u2019eau et de nutriments dans le m\u00eame  massif. Assurez-vous de pr\u00e9parer le sol en enlevant les  mauvaises herbes, en ajoutant des amendements de sol si n\u00e9cessaire et en  nivelant le sol pour une meilleure circulation de l\u2019eau.   4 \u2013 Ne pas suivre les recommandations de  plantation : Chaque plante a des recommandations sp\u00e9cifiques en mati\u00e8re  de profondeur de plantation et d\u2019espacement. En \u00e9vitant ces erreurs courantes, vous  pouvez cr\u00e9er un massif de plantes sain et florissant qui ajoutera de la  beaut\u00e9 et de la vie \u00e0 votre jardin. Il existe environ 210 esp\u00e8ces de magnolias diff\u00e9rentes, qui  sont originaires d\u2019Asie, d\u2019Am\u00e9rique du Nord et d\u2019Am\u00e9rique centrale. Cette  plante est populaire dans les jardins et les parcs en raison de sa  beaut\u00e9 et de son parfum agr\u00e9able. Les fleurs de magnolia ont des p\u00e9tales  \u00e9pais et charnus, qui peuvent \u00eatre blancs, roses, rouges, pourpres ou  jaunes, selon l\u2019esp\u00e8ce. \u00c9galement  connus pour leur importance culturelle et historique. Les premiers  fossiles de magnolias ont \u00e9t\u00e9 trouv\u00e9s remontant \u00e0 plus de 100 millions  d\u2019ann\u00e9es, et ils ont \u00e9t\u00e9 utilis\u00e9s \u00e0 des fins m\u00e9dicinales et  c\u00e9r\u00e9monielles dans de nombreuses cultures \u00e0 travers le monde. Chacune  des vari\u00e9t\u00e9s de magnolia a ses propres caract\u00e9ristiques et exigences de  croissance. Voici quelques-unes des vari\u00e9t\u00e9s de magnolias les plus  utilis\u00e9es dans les jardins : Magnolia grandiflora : aussi connu sous le nom de magnolia \u00e0  grandes feuilles, c\u2019est une esp\u00e8ce \u00e0 feuilles persistantes avec des  fleurs blanches tr\u00e8s parfum\u00e9es. Il est couramment utilis\u00e9 comme arbre  d\u2019ornement dans les climats chauds.   Magnolia soulangeana : \u00e9galement connu sous le nom de magnolia  de Soulange, c\u2019est une esp\u00e8ce \u00e0 feuilles caduques avec de grandes fleurs  roses et blanches en forme de coupe. Il est souvent utilis\u00e9 dans les  massifs ou les haies.   Magnolia stellata : aussi connu sous le nom de magnolia \u00e9toil\u00e9,  c\u2019est une esp\u00e8ce \u00e0 feuilles caduques avec de petites fleurs blanches en  forme d\u2019\u00e9toile. Il est souvent utilis\u00e9 dans les jardins japonais ou  pour les plantations en pot.   Magnolia liliiflora : \u00e9galement connu sous le nom de magnolia de Lily, c\u2019est une esp\u00e8ce \u00e0 feuilles caduques avec des fleurs roses fonc\u00e9es en forme de tulipe. Il est souvent utilis\u00e9 dans les massifs ou comme arbre solitaire.   Magnolia sieboldii : aussi connu sous le nom de magnolia de  Siebold, c\u2019est une esp\u00e8ce \u00e0 feuilles caduques avec des fleurs blanches  ou roses p\u00e2les. Il est souvent utilis\u00e9 dans les jardins japonais ou les  massifs.   Le Magnolia peut \u00eatre utilis\u00e9 de diff\u00e9rentes mani\u00e8res dans un jardin, en  fonction de la vari\u00e9t\u00e9 et de la taille de l\u2019arbre ou de l\u2019arbuste.  Voici quelques id\u00e9es d\u2019utilisation : Comme arbre d\u2019ornement : Les magnolias sont souvent plant\u00e9s comme arbres  d\u2019ornement, en raison de leur beaut\u00e9 et de leur parfum. Ils peuvent  \u00eatre plant\u00e9s en tant qu\u2019arbre solitaire ou en groupe pour former une  all\u00e9e ou une haie.   En massif : Les magnolias peuvent \u00e9galement \u00eatre utilis\u00e9s pour cr\u00e9er des  massifs dans un jardin. Les vari\u00e9t\u00e9s plus petites peuvent \u00eatre plant\u00e9es  en groupe pour cr\u00e9er un massif fleuri et parfum\u00e9.  En association avec d\u2019autres plantes : Les magnolias peuvent \u00eatre  associ\u00e9s \u00e0 d\u2019autres plantes pour cr\u00e9er un jardin diversifi\u00e9 et color\u00e9.  Par exemple, ils peuvent \u00eatre plant\u00e9s avec des azal\u00e9es, des  rhododendrons et des cam\u00e9lias pour cr\u00e9er un jardin d\u2019inspiration  asiatique.   En pot : Les vari\u00e9t\u00e9s naines peuvent \u00eatre plant\u00e9es en pot pour ajouter de la couleur et du parfum sur un patio ou une terrasse.   En topiaire : Les magnolias peuvent \u00eatre taill\u00e9s en topiaire pour cr\u00e9er des formes int\u00e9ressantes dans un jardin. Il  y a beaucoup d\u2019esp\u00e8ces et vari\u00e9t\u00e9s de magnolias, chacune ayant sa  propre beaut\u00e9 et caract\u00e9ristiques. title: help please re:- Flooring | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-43564809", "author_name": "HU-43564809", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43564809", "date": "2023-03-29", "text": "Our house was built in 1904 and the back kitchen has quarry tiles in it. We are knocking down walls and as a consequence the new layout means the floor will need replacing. Different builders give us different advice regarding how to deal with the tiles. We don\u2019t want to keep the quarry tiles as the kitchen is cold. Some say we can screed over it and some say dig it all up and lay a new floor with a DPC. Can someone advise what is the best cause of action as we don\u2019t want to end up with severe damp up the walls. Any help or advice would really be gratefully appreciated.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "minnie101", "author_name": "minnie101", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/minnie101", "date": "2023-03-29", "text": "I don\u2019t know if this helps? https://www.homebuilding.co.uk/advice/renovating-old-floors", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-43564809", "author_name": "HU-43564809", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43564809", "date": "2023-03-29", "text": "Thank you for the link", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "hzdeleted-75719626", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-75719626", "date": "2023-03-30", "text": "What kind of flooring are you hoping to get installed? The builders who recommend to screed over the quarry tiles, what kind of flooring do they recommend putting on top of the concrete? Is that going to make the floor less cold? Without a DPC, isn't there going to be a risk of efflorescence? You'll still have to deal with vapour coming up through the floor, so you'll be limited in the kind of flooring you can use. I doubt you could put vinyl flooring without a vapour barrier, but I'm not sure. I'm not an expert, but (assuming your floor is original) unless you insulate the floor, it will continue to be cold. And to insulate the floor, you will have to dig it out unless you have enough head room to raise it. You could potentially install a wooden floor so it doesn't feel as cold, but it would need breathing room underneath to avoid damage from the ground moisture. You could also add vapour-permeable insulation underneath. As for DPC causing damp walls, what do the builders recommending it say about that? My understanding is that you could put a drainage system on the inside of the house, under the slab, (example: https://hammerandhand.com/best-practices/manual/7-basements/7-4-basement-retrofit/). It might still be a good idea to insulate the floor to avoid condensation issues. I would personally consider a proper DPC to decrease the humidity inside the house, especially in a humid climate, but it's an expensive intervention. As water turns into vapour, it uses up energy (heat) and cools down the air. Without a DPC, the more you heat your place, the more water from the ground turns into vapour and gets into your house, so it's not very energy efficient.", "images": []}}

Do we ask for samples in the room and the hall or just the room? Color - These floors are in a studio guest apartment down the hall from our main apartment. The same company did the floors in the main apartment before we moved in and it is almost certainly Minwax.  When I hold up the Minwax samples to our floor, the Minwax has more red and brown undertones.  Our floor has more blond undertones. title: Is it my water? Years-long mystery | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "cristina-s37", "author_name": "Artist-FKA-Novice Zone 7B GA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cristina-s37", "date": "2023-03-30", "text": "I've been having this problem for years now. In fact, I have asked about it here before but I still haven't figured out the issue. Over time, all of my AV-s gradually turn tight, with very hard leaves. Eventually they become stunted. I provide all the right care, including watering, adequate light, fertilizing, humidity, etc. For a while I thought I may be using too much fertilizer but I really don't think this is the problem. I use Jack's for AV-s - a diluted solution each time I water. I follow their instructions for \"every time you water,\" 1/4 tsp per gallon. Sometimes I have used some orchid fert too - but I really don't think this is the culprit. And no, there are no pests. Through the process of elimination, the only possible explanation I was left with is my water. It turns out we do have hard water; in fact it is so hard that it has been the cause of many older pipes bursting in our area and I heard some people even considered suing the county. However, I read that AV-s can be OK with hard water and may even be able to use some of the minerals there. Is that true? Even so, mine may be too hard. It would make intuitive sense to imagine the plant slowly absorbing too much mineral matter and eventually turning rigid and tight as a result. How should I go about testing this theory? I am thinking to take them off the tap water and set them on a distilled water or spring water regimen, with no fert at first, to  see if I notice a change in culture. At the same time, I don't want to deprive them of bloom. If so, should I just switch to bottled water and continue with the fertilizer as always? Any opinion/advice would be greatly appreciated.", "images": []}

title: Query regarding our cavity wall insulation specification | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-344389367", "author_name": "HU-344389367", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-344389367", "date": "2023-03-30", "text": "We're currently having an extension built, builders on site preparing the footing and brickwork starting in a week or so, but I've hit a problem with our cavity walls specs. On the architect drawings (top down plans and structure cross-section) it shows 100mm facing brick, 100mm cavity, 100m blockwork (then normal plasterboard). All of the floorplan measurements are based on this size of cavity wall for the whole build. Our builder (who I have complete faith in) however says that the plans are wrong, it shuold have an additional 90mm of insulation board on all internal facing walls.... this has come as a shock as of course we agreed to the plans and had planning permission approved for what's on the plans. The new kitchen we've had planned and ordered will need to be redone, and the rooms are now 180mm (90mm each side) smaller floorspace than we were expecting. All this has only come to light right when the work is fully underway. With the plans, our architect included a \"General Notes\" page which includes this regarding the cavity walls: \"6.0 EXTERNAL WALLS: (max 0.18W/m2k U-value) 315mm nominal cavity work, finished in facing brickwork. 100mm facing brickwork, 100mm full fill cavity insulation cavity with 90mm 'Kingspan Kooltherm K106' (0.021 W/mk) foil-backed extruded insulation to internal face (continued min 150mm below ground floor insulation level) and maintain 50mm clear cavity, 100mm Celcon Standard (0.15 Wmk) blockwork 3.5N/mm2 finished internally with 2 coat 13mm plaster.\" Before I contact our architect and try and find out what went wrong here, can anyone confirm whether the above tallies with what our builder is saying? I also feel as though surely the local Planning department should have picked up on this conflict. Can anyone offer advice on what options there might be to try and reduce the size of these walls? Are there thinner options available for example with the same thermal properties? This is a very standard south-facing kitchen / diner extension, really nothing fancy at all.", "images": []}

title: Wearing braces as an "older person" ... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "idaclaire2", "author_name": "Ida Claire", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/idaclaire2", "date": "2023-03-30", "text": "At a relatively overdue dental exam yesterday, my longtime and trusted dentist told me that she believed I would benefit from braces due to a shift in my teeth over time that's now causing a bite problem and a couple of other issues.  It's not something I've been particularly aware of until recently, when I can detect that my lower teeth are more crowded and crooked than before, and I often have a sensation in my jaw -- not pain or aching, but more like a kind of continual pressure.  The dentist said yep, my shifting teeth is the cause of those things.  She provided a referral to an ortho (he seems pretty impressive -- board-certified with decades of experience and glowing reviews and professional accolades), and I have an appointment to go see him for a consultation in a few weeks.  My dentist and I discussed Invisalign, but she believes I would be a better candidate for braces, as they can be tweaked to better adjust each tooth individually.  I have three uppers that have actually twisted a bit. I'm certainly not embarrassed of my smile and I believe my issues are probably mild compared to some of the before/after photos I've seen -- so I wouldn't be pursuing this for \"vanity\", but because I want my teeth to last me a good long while as I move into my 60s and beyond.  I guess if it's something that will enhance my overall dental health, I will likely proceed if the recommendation is to do so by the orthodontist.  After reading a good deal online already, I do get a vague sense that \"adult orthodontia\" is a relatively new and perhaps trendy thing, but that may be because there are a host of boomers and others a bit younger who are aging but still active and looking forward to continued health, who want to do whatever they can to preserve their natural teeth.  It wasn't an option for folks just one or two generations ago. This leads me to ask if anyone here wears or wore braces as an adult, or if you have a spouse or adult family member who has and can speak to the overall experience.  Particularly, I'm interested in knowing:", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2023-04-01", "text": "There is a physiologic/anthropological reason for the tooth crowding that occurs in the lower anterior, and it is also related to the reason we often do not have room for our wisdom teeth. Prehistorically we ate a lot of abrasives with our food and our teeth wore down. If you think of teeth being shaped essentially like ice cream cones, as the teeth wear down they get narrower. They would shift forward and toward the middle to close the spaces so our gums did not get damaged. Then partway through live we would get another molar in back to help with grinding and then we would die. Now we eat much softer food, our lives are much longer and our mandibles are getting smaller, They still move toward the center but don't wear them down and the front teeth have small enough contact points that they can shift past each other and overlap.", "images": []}}

Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. title: Fast Food outside the U.S. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "fawnridge69", "author_name": "fawnridge (Ricky)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fawnridge69", "date": "2023-03-30", "text": "As a frequent world traveler, I've had the opportunity over the years to try fast food in other countries. Now, before I go any further, I NEVER eat fast food. However, curiosity has frequently gotten the better of me and I've sampled the wares of various chains. For example: There's a McDonald's in Paris on the north side of the Arch de Triomphe that has a world class chocolate shake. It's not the standard mix that's used everywhere else. The manager uses his own blend of chocolate and it's amazing. The funny thing is that there's another McDonald's on the south side of the famous arch and their milk shakes are the standard crap. KFC in Jamaica is radically different than the Colonel's offerings in the States. The chicken is all free-range, locally sourced and they use a dry rub that has some serious heat for the extra crispy. I've eaten in three different KFCs in Jamaica and they're all the same and much better than the US version. I was in Ecuador many years ago and had Taco Bell at a mall. They also had dozens of other fast food joints in the same food court, but everyone was lined up for tacos. It took almost 30 minutes to get to the counter, but they were as good as any tacos I've eaten from the trucks by the fields in Florida. Several years ago, the rage in Amsterdam was French fries. Seeing lines of 50 to 100 people, I just had to taste them for myself. Forget about McD's fries, supposedly the best in the world, the three places I bought them in Amsterdam rocked! Perfectly fried, not greasy at all, and just the right about of seasoning. One more. British food takes its knocks, until you try Burger King. Wow! Talk about your perfect hamburger. This Austin is meant to stay small and she does. Mine is still about 2.5X2.5 feet and grows in a near perfect shape, requiring little pruning. Tamora is a parent of Evelyn and other excellent roses. She has the so called Myrrh scent, but I couldn't describe, though I like it. She came from Pickering in Canada and is grafted on multiflora rootstock. Most of my Austins are huge, but Tamora is small, never throwing out gangly canes. During that time get used to your home, keep a notebook listing the things that work well and the things you would like to change.  Learn your new budget, create a budget to save for the big expenses that will come down the pike (new roof, new furnace, new hot water heater, new appliances).  Rule of thumb is to save 1% of your homes value for annual maintenance and 1% of your homes value for big ticket repairs per year.   If you just spent $300,000 on a new home that means you need to save $250 per month toward maintenance and repairs and $250 per month for major repairs.   Once that is taken care of you can determine a savings plan for furniture.  It also has to be replaced or recovered as it gets worn. While figuring out what you love and hate about your new home you can figure out the perfect style and types of furniture that will fit your lifestyle.    If you are more likely to have a wine and cheese party and entertain your boss at home you may appreciate a more formal living space.  If you have football parties with beer and pizza you may prefer something more casual. Think about the colors you love and what kinds of art make your heart sing. We all look at online pictures and magazines and those professional photos often look great, but you don't live in the pages of a magazine.   If you are not a minimalist, creating a minimalist home isn't going to make you a minimalist and your going to be fighting your need for things and the design you picked.   If you really are natured to be a minimalist and you get some beautiful, heavily carved Queen Anne furniture you may be overwhelmed with how busy it all ends up. If you pick whatever is most popular today, you will find yourself with a home that is dated.     By figuring out what works best for you and what you want now and will still love 10 years from now and 20 years from now will save you a lot of time and money.    Accept that you will make some mistakes, but through good planning you will make fewer mistakes and smaller mistakes. Remember this is a marathon.   You will be decorating your home over the next 40-50 years.   It doesn't all have to be done today.   Take your time and shop for those items that you love.  Wait for sales, buy good used furniture rather than cheap new furniture.  Plan on replacing 2 or 3 items every year until you have your home filled with things you love. Enjoy the process and remember the most important function of your home is being the place where your child is forming the memories that will last them a lifetime. At age 61 I don't think back to my childhood home and think \"I loved the color of my bedroom.\"   I think back and remember laying on our sofa with my head on my mom's lap and her running her fingers through my hair while she told me stories of when she was young. title: Connaissez-vous l’origine du métier d’ébéniste ? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "atelier-drouin-pfvwus-pf~1262607302", "author_name": "Atelier Drouin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/woodworkers-and-carpenters/atelier-drouin-pfvwus-pf~1262607302", "date": "2023-03-31", "text": "ORIGINES DU M\u00c9TIER Le bois est utilis\u00e9 depuis l\u2019Antiquit\u00e9. Les \u00c9gyptiens honoraient leurs morts en r\u00e9alisant, entre autres, des ouvrages pr\u00e9cieux en bois \u00e0 destination des pyramides. En Europe, c\u2019est au moyen \u00e2ge que l\u2019on identifie les premiers mobiliers en bois. En France, le terme \u00ab \u00e9b\u00e9nisterie \u00bb appara\u00eet en 1732 dans le dictionnaire de l\u2019Acad\u00e9mie fran\u00e7aise. Les \u00e9changes commerciaux se d\u00e9veloppant, les artisans importent des bois rares et pr\u00e9cieux. Toutefois, plut\u00f4t que de fabriquer un meuble en bois massif, ils ont l\u2019id\u00e9e disruptive de plaquer sur du ch\u00eane ou du noyer, des fines feuilles des arbres qu\u2019ils rapportent par bateau, dont le fameux \u00ab \u00e9b\u00e8ne \u00bb. C\u2019est ainsi que nait le m\u00e9tier d\u2019\u00e9b\u00e9niste et qui permet aux seigneurs de poss\u00e9der des meubles d\u2019apparat pour un co\u00fbt bien moins on\u00e9reux ! ESSOR DU M\u00c9TIER Le m\u00e9tier d\u2019\u00e9b\u00e9niste prend son essor sous le r\u00e8gne de Louis XIV. Un \u00e9b\u00e9niste de renom, Andr\u00e9- Charles Boulle, travaille \u00e0 Versailles et innove en cr\u00e9ant du mobilier en placage d\u2019\u00e9b\u00e8ne qu\u2019il associe \u00e0 du laiton et de l\u2019\u00e9caille de tortue.   Par son d\u00e9veloppement, le m\u00e9tier d\u2019\u00e9b\u00e9niste contribue au rayonnement d\u2019un style \u00e0 la fran\u00e7aise \u00e0 travers toute l\u2019Europe. A chaque r\u00e8gne et / ou \u00e9poque correspond un style de mobilier particulier. Les \u00e9b\u00e9nistes deviennent des artisans d\u2019Art capables de travailler diff\u00e9rents mat\u00e9riaux comme la nacre, l\u2019ivoire, l\u2019os, l\u2019\u00e9tain, le laiton, l\u2019\u00e9caille, le galuchat \u2026 \u00e0 des fins d\u2019ornementation. LA RESTAURATION DE MOBILIER \u00c9b\u00e9niste \u00e0 Paris, Atelier DROUIN intervient pour un des aspects du m\u00e9tier qu\u2019est la restauration de mobilier ancien et d\u2019objets d\u2019art. La restauration de meubles requiert une fine connaissance du bois, des mat\u00e9riaux cit\u00e9s plus avant et des styles et techniques propres \u00e0 chaque \u00e9poque. En effet, l\u2019enjeu est avant tout de pr\u00e9server l\u2019authenticit\u00e9 d\u2019un meuble, en utilisant les vernis appropri\u00e9s (gomme laque versus polyur\u00e9thane) ou colles ad\u00e9quates : colles animales (poisson, os, nerf) versus les colles blanches, r\u00e9sines. Avant d\u2019agir, le restaurateur de mobilier prend donc le temps d\u2019analyser le style, l\u2019\u00e9poque et les mat\u00e9riaux utilis\u00e9s pour diagnostiquer pr\u00e9cis\u00e9ment les raisons de la d\u00e9t\u00e9rioration et ainsi proposer les solutions les plus pertinentes. Toute action doit pouvoir \u00eatre r\u00e9versible, sans abimer le meuble. L\u2019ignorance de certains praticiens a pu engendrer une d\u00e9t\u00e9rioration accrue de meubles qui auraient n\u00e9cessit\u00e9 un plus grand respect des techniques et mat\u00e9riaux d\u2019origine. Cette superbe m\u00e9nag\u00e8re Art D\u00e9co en \u00e9b\u00e8ne de Macassar est dot\u00e9e de poign\u00e9es en ivoire, mati\u00e8re prot\u00e9g\u00e9e. Il a fallu employer le plus grand soin pour les nettoyer avec des produits naturels.
